questions.q: A body of mass $m$ is at rest on a rough horizontal surface. A force less than the limiting friction is applied. The friction acting is:
questions.solution:
Static friction is **self-adjusting**: it takes whatever value is needed to keep the body at rest, up to a maximum $\mu_s N$.

Since the body does not move, the net force is zero, so friction exactly balances the applied force.

Only once the applied force exceeds $\mu_s N$ does the body slide, and friction then drops to the kinetic value $\mu_k N$.

questions.q: A lift accelerates upward at $a$. The apparent weight of a person of mass $m$ inside is:
questions.solution:
Apparent weight is the normal reaction $N$ from the floor.

Taking up as positive, Newton's second law for the person:

$N - mg = ma \Rightarrow N = \mathbf{m(g + a)}$.

Accelerating downward gives $m(g - a)$, and in free fall ($a = g$) the reaction is zero — weightlessness.

questions.q: A block just begins to slide down an incline when the angle of inclination is $\theta$. The coefficient of static friction is:
questions.solution:
At the point of sliding, the component of weight along the incline equals the limiting friction:

$mg\sin\theta = \mu_s N = \mu_s\,mg\cos\theta$

$\mu_s = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \mathbf{\tan\theta}$.

$\theta$ is called the angle of repose. Notice the mass cancels — a heavy block and a light one slip at the same angle.

options: Act on different bodies and cancel
Act on different bodies and never cancel
questions.solution:
Newton's third law pairs are equal, opposite, and act on **different** bodies.

Because they act on different bodies they can never cancel each other — cancellation only makes sense for forces on the *same* body.

That is why a horse can pull a cart: the forward force on the cart and the backward force on the horse act on different objects.

questions.q: A car takes a circular turn of radius $r$ on a level road with coefficient of friction $\mu$. The maximum safe speed is:
questions.solution:
Friction supplies the centripetal force:

$\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} \le \mu mg$

$v^{2} \le \mu r g \Rightarrow v_{\max} = \mathbf{\sqrt{\mu r g}}$.

The mass cancels — a loaded lorry and an empty one skid at the same speed on the same bend.

questions.q: A bullet of mass $m$ leaves a gun of mass $M$ with speed $v$. The recoil speed of the gun is:
questions.solution:
Momentum is conserved: the system starts at rest, so the total momentum stays zero.

$0 = mv + MV \Rightarrow V = -\dfrac{mv}{M}$.

The magnitude of the recoil is $\mathbf{mv/M}$, and the minus sign says it is opposite to the bullet.

A heavy gun recoils slowly, which is why artillery pieces are massive.

questions.q: Two masses $m_1 > m_2$ hang from a light string over a frictionless pulley. The acceleration of the system is:
questions.solution:
Take the direction of motion as positive for each mass and let $T$ be the tension.

For $m_1$ (descending): $m_1 g - T = m_1 a$

For $m_2$ (rising): $T - m_2 g = m_2 a$

Adding eliminates $T$:

$(m_1 - m_2)g = (m_1 + m_2)a \Rightarrow a = \mathbf{\dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}}$.

This is Atwood's machine; equal masses give $a = 0$, as they must.

questions.q: A cricketer moves his hands backwards while catching a ball in order to:
options: Increase the time of impact and so reduce the force
questions.solution:
The change in momentum is fixed — the ball must be brought to rest either way.

Impulse $= F\,\Delta t = \Delta p$. With $\Delta p$ fixed, increasing $\Delta t$ **reduces** $F$.

Drawing the hands back stretches the collision over a longer time, so the force on the hands is smaller. The same principle is behind crumple zones and airbags.

It takes a larger force to *start* a body sliding than to *keep* it sliding, so

$\mu_k < \mu_s$.

The microscopic picture is that a stationary contact settles into interlocked asperities which must be broken; once moving, the surfaces skate over one another with less interlocking.

This is why a pushed crate lurches forward the moment it breaks free.

questions.q: A force of $20\ \text{N}$ acts on a body of mass $4\ \text{kg}$ at rest on a frictionless surface. Find its speed, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, after $3\ \text{s}$.
A $10\ \text{kg}$ block on a horizontal surface has $\mu_k = 0.2$. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, find the kinetic friction force, in newtons.
questions.solution:
On a horizontal surface the normal reaction is $N = mg = 10 \times 10 = 100\ \text{N}$.

$f_k = \mu_k N = 0.2 \times 100 = \mathbf{20\ \text{N}}$.

questions.q: A $0.2\ \text{kg}$ ball moving at $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ strikes a wall normally and rebounds at $8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find the magnitude of the impulse, in $\mathrm{N\,s}$.
questions.solution:
Take the initial direction as positive. The ball rebounds, so its final velocity is $-8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$\Delta p = m(v - u) = 0.2\,(-8 - 10) = 0.2 \times (-18) = -3.6\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

The magnitude is $\mathbf{3.6\ \mathrm{N\,s}}$.

The sign reversal is what makes a rebound impulse larger than a dead stop would be.

questions.q: A stone of mass $0.5\ \text{kg}$ is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius $2\ \text{m}$ at $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find the tension in the string, in newtons.
questions.solution:
In a horizontal circle the string tension provides the centripetal force:

$T = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{0.5 \times 4^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{0.5 \times 16}{2} = \dfrac{8}{2} = \mathbf{4\ \text{N}}$.

questions.q: Masses of $6\ \text{kg}$ and $4\ \text{kg}$ hang over a frictionless pulley. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, find the acceleration, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Derive the expression for the maximum safe speed of a vehicle on a road banked at angle $\theta$, with coefficient of friction $\mu$ between tyres and road. Hence obtain the speed for which no friction is needed, and explain why roads are banked.
questions.solution:
**Setting up.** Let the vehicle of mass $m$ move in a circle of radius $r$ on a road banked at $\theta$. Three forces act: the weight $mg$ down, the normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the road surface, and friction $f$ along the surface.

At maximum speed the vehicle tends to slide *outwards* and *up* the slope, so friction acts **down** the slope, $f = \mu N$.

**Resolving.** Vertically (no vertical acceleration):

$N\cos\theta = mg + \mu N\sin\theta$

Horizontally (towards the centre, supplying the centripetal force):

$N\sin\theta + \mu N\cos\theta = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$

**Dividing** the second by the first to eliminate $N$ and $m$:

$\dfrac{\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu\sin\theta} = \dfrac{v^{2}}{rg}$

Dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$:

$v_{\max} = \sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\tan\theta + \mu}{1 - \mu\tan\theta}\right)}$

**The frictionless speed.** Setting $\mu = 0$:

$v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$

At exactly this speed the horizontal component of the normal reaction alone supplies the centripetal force, and no friction is called on at all.

**Why roads are banked.** On a level road the whole centripetal force must come from friction, which is unreliable — it falls sharply when the road is wet, icy or dusty. Banking makes a component of the normal reaction do the work instead, so the turn stays safe when friction cannot be counted on, and a much higher speed is possible for the same radius. Railway tracks are canted for the same reason.
